edges.effect_quant: In older adults, loop diuretics consistently track with hypokalemia and related electrolyte instability. In a 36,361-patient geriatric screening study, loop diuretics were an independent risk factor for community-acquired hypokalemia. Earlier geriatric admission studies also found loop or thiazide diuretic exposure associated independently with lower serum potassium, and diuretic users had lower sodium and higher urea and creatinine than nonusers.
edges.population: older adults, especially those aged 65 years or older who are prescribed loop diuretics such as furosemide for heart failure or volume management
edges.mechanism: Loop diuretics increase urinary sodium, potassium, and magnesium losses while also provoking volume shifts that can worsen azotemia and dysnatremia in susceptible older adults. Age-related renal vulnerability, comorbidity burden, and concurrent medications amplify those electrolyte effects.
edges.summary: This is a credible harmful medication-safety edge in geriatrics. The literature most consistently points to potassium loss, but broader sodium and renal chemistry disturbances are also more common in older diuretic users, particularly when renal function is reduced or multiple comorbidities are present.
edges.caveats: Some observational studies group loop and thiazide diuretics together or compare several preparations at once, so not every risk estimate is loop-specific. Even so, the repeated direction of association and the underlying renal physiology make a harmful interpretation much stronger than a neutral one.
